messages.body_plain:
Hello Dirk and everyone,

when I did my first assessment of the impact of the mass architecture
restriction of Bioc and CRAN packages, I assumed that all of Dirk's
source package names were not starting with "r-cran", and therefore
strongly underestimated their number, and therefore the impact on Dirk.

Dirk, I apologise to you for this error.

I have browsed the planned autoremoval page
(https://udd.debian.org/cgi-bin/autoremovals.cgi), looking at which of
the team-maintained r-cran-* packages are responsible for most of the
impact on Dirk's packages.  Without surprise, most of them are related
to the tidyverse or provide other services that are not scientific
computations (r-cran-jpeg, r-cran-jsonlite, etc.).

Our routine-update restricts architectures by default but I have
added a list of exceptions, which I am uploading now.

https://salsa.debian.org/debian/routine-update/-/blob/c21f890155726d72362ba50e5939dfc261dec3bc/routine-update#L599

The list of exceptions is still growing, but I want to keep it short
with the two following criteria:

 - A large number of packages depend or transitively depend on the
   package getting an exception.
 - The package is not performing scientific computations.

Dirk, these excptions will considerably reduce the list of packages for
which I would like to ask you to add architecture-is-64-bit,
architecture-is-little-endian, in their Build-Depends field.  I do not
yet have a list but it will probably include car, effects, lme4 and
r-cran-pbkrtest for instance, as they depend on r-cran-statmod.

Have a nice day,

Charles

Hi Graham and Dirk,

Le Sat, Apr 04, 2026 at 12:18:52PM +0000, Graham Inggs a écrit :
> 
> Is r-cran-statmod a particularly troublesome package to build everywhere?

The difficulty we face is that, on architectures without upstream regression
testing, bugs appear randomly and unpredictably. In my view, this makes the
workload unsustainable given the resources we currently have. This is not about
r-cran-statmod specifically but about the entire collection. At some point we
need to draw a line, rather than continue playing whack‑a‑mole with porting
issues that can seize our time without warning.

We could, of course, stop running regression tests altogether or mask the
issues by disabling failing tests, as has occasionally been done in the past.
But that approach goes against Debian’s standards, which increasingly emphasize
reproducibility and reliability.

Dirk, I have read and understood your comments about CRAN being well tested and
not requiring re-testing on amd64 and arm64—the architectures you target with
r2u. However, on the other architectures, autopkgtests do uncover real bugs,
and these may well be only the tip of the iceberg.

If we are serious about supporting Debian on these other architectures, my view
is that we should aim to distribute packages that genuinely work there, and
avoid shipping packages that we already suspect to be less reliable than on
amd64.

> car and effects are architecture all

Sorry, I did not check before writing.  This is good news and less work.

> adding Build-Depends on architecture-is-64-bit and
> architecture-is-little-endian doesn't do what you think it does.

I understand that it is useless and ugly to upload the arch-all packages with
these build-depends, but it is also harmless and was simplest for me since it
was done in a loop of automated uploads.

> Secondly, if you do end up removing the binaries of r-cran-statmod on some
> architectures, then lme4 and r-cran-pbkrtest will no longer be able to build
> on those architectures, and all you need to do is also request removal of the
> binaries of lme4 and r-cran-pbkrtest.

That is excellent news, thank for pointing it out to me.  I will fill removal
requests for r-cran-statmod and let Dirk know what removal requests are needed
on his side.  Dirk, if you want me to fill the architecture removal requests
on your behalf, please let me know.

> design mistake in how autopkgtests are set up, casting too wide a net by

Most if not all of the removal requests at the moment are because of the
architecture restrictions and not of the autopkgtests.

perspective, and I understand yours. I’m not yet sure where the release team
stands on this. If they ask me to proceed in the way you suggest, I will do so.
If we ultimately end up with three different viewpoints, I propose bringing the
matter to the technical committee at a later stage. I will accept their

Have a nice week-end,

On 5 April 2026 at 00:28, Charles Plessy wrote:
| Dirk, I have read and understood your comments about CRAN being well tested and
| not requiring re-testing on amd64 and arm64—the architectures you target with
| r2u. However, on the other architectures, autopkgtests do uncover real bugs,
| and these may well be only the tip of the iceberg.

You continue to not hear what I am saying. [ I am not saying Debian should
mimick r2u which is an illustration showing that it is in fact easy to script
builds of CRAN package at larger scale. And that there is demand for working
_and current_ packages. ]

Let me try again. My position is that the cross product of testing over

  - a large-ish number 'N' of packages (I guess we are 1300 or so r-{cran,bioc}-*)
  - times all our 'A' build architectures
  - times all possible dependency packages

creates a problem set that is too large and not meaningful.

We are Debian, so of course we look after the packages picked ('N') and
platforms we support ('A'). We all agree here.

Where your view differs from mine (and also from what e.g. Paul Gevers
clearly stated in some threads shared between the BTS and this list) is
whether it is wise to run autopkgtest across all three dimension (ie
including all Suggests).  My *core position* is that that is not wise.

My recommendations remains to NOT extend autopkgtest to ALL SUGGESTED
packages.  Run 'all package N times all architectures A across all hard
dependencies'.  Discover bugs, contact upstream, that alone may keep you busy
giving that there seem to be few other active debian-r maintainers. You could
then selectively turn on more extended tests and file bugs with upstream.
That would make use of Debian's infrastructure, but without overly
constraining ourselves.

In the meantime, R 4.6.0 will come out at the end of April and my prediction
is that this ongoing quagmire will prevent it from migrating to testing for
no fault of its own just as your activities have removed several of my
r-cran-* packages for no real reason from testing. Really not a great look.

Dirk

On 5 April 2026 at 23:39, Aurelien Jarno wrote:
| It appears that the issue is that r-cran is using NaN boxing to 
| represent the NA value. This does not work on riscv64, as a canonical 
| NaN is generated for an operation involving a NaN input operand.

Yes, well spotted. There are a few issues going on. For context:

- R itself natively only has double (64bit) and int (32bit). We often want
  int64_t and there is an add-on package 'mocking' int64 via an underlying
  double (package 'bit64', used by 'data.table' and many others)

- double is all good because of IEE 754 so NA, NaN, ... are defined.  But R
  is a data language and wants NA, NaN, ... on other types and hence 'locally
  defines' NA for int effectively dropping one value, also for bool making
  bool 'TRUE', 'FALSE' or 'NA' and character.

- for int64 we generally get by (see below), but it appears that the usual
  ops lead on riscv64 to a NA turning into a NaN. And instead of testing
  'is.finite()' where both come out FALSE data.table appears to only looks at
  NA here.   Adjusting that may fix the bug. I am sure upstream gets to that,
  they started to comment / ask for more feedback here
    https://github.com/Rdatatable/data.table/issues/7695
  and maybe you can help?

Dirk

Simple example (on my amd64 box)

  > vals <- c(1.12, 42L, NA, NaN)  # vector of 'double', int gets cast up
  > vals
  [1]  1.12 42.00    NA   NaN
  > as.integer64(vals)    # make them 'int64' (needs bit64 package)
  integer64
  [1] 1    42   <NA> <NA>
  > is.na(as.integer64(vals))
  [1] FALSE FALSE  TRUE  TRUE
  > is.finite(as.integer64(vals))
  [1]  TRUE  TRUE FALSE FALSE
  >

Hello,

we run lintian-brush on the r-cran-* packages maintained by the Debian R
packages maintainers team, and I noted that recenly the UDD reports a
lot of uscan errors for our packages. 

The reason is that lintian-brush converts files like this:

    --- a/debian/watch
    +++ b/debian/watch
    @@ -1,2 +1,3 @@
    -version=4
    -https://cloud.r-project.org/src/contrib/forecast_([-\d.]*)\.tar\.gz
    +Version: 5
    +
    +Source: https://cloud.r-project.org/src/contrib/forecast_([-\d.]*)\.tar\.gz

But the new watch file is broken:

    $ uscan --report
    uscan warn: No Matching-Pattern found, using .*?@ANY_VERSION@@ARCHIVE_EXT@
    uscan warn: In debian/watch no matching files for watch source
      https://cloud.r-project.org/src/contrib/forecast_([-\d.]*)\.tar\.gz

While the old one would have worked:

    $ uscan --report
    Newest version of r-cran-forecast on remote site is 9.0.2, local version is 9.0.1
     => Newer package available from:
    	=> https://cloud.r-project.org/src/contrib/forecast_9.0.2.tar.gz

By the way, since devscripts 2.26.6, we have a uscan template for CRAN
and Bioconductor packages, so the following watch file would work:

    Version: 5
    Template: CRAN
    Package: forecast

Would that something that lintian-brush could implement?  All CRAN
packages come from https://cloud.r-project.org/, and all Bioconductor
packages come from https://bioconductor.org/.

Have a nice day,

Charles

messages.subject: R 4.6 in unstable: testing migration and autopkgtest implications
messages.subject_clean: R 4.6 in unstable: testing migration and autopkgtest implications
messages.body_plain:
Hello everybody,

As you know R 4.6.0 release candidates are currently shipped in unstable
(r-base 4.5.3.20260417-1 and later). As part of this, the R graphics engine ABI
has been bumped (graphics API 16 → 17) and other incompatibilities are being
uncovered.  While no transition has been declared, the transition is already
effective in the archive.

Impact on testing migration;

 * Some important binary r-cran- packages built against R ≤ 4.5 (notably
   r-cran-rlang and r-cran-vctrs) are incompatible with r-base shipping R 4.6,
   and vice‑versa.

 * During unstable → testing migration, britney runs autopkgtests against
   partial upgrades by design. Since these incompatibilities are not fully
   declared, reverse‑dependency tests triggered by r-base and by r-cran- core
   packages fail, blocking migration.

 * r-cran-rlang autopkgtests detect this correctly. I added a versioned Breaks
   against r-base-core, but this is insufficient to prevent invalid mixed
   testing/unstable combinations for its reverse dependencies.

 * r-cran-vctrs is similarly blocked, in addition to at least one riscv64
   regression triggered during migration.

 * Independently, the current r-cran-rcpp in unstable is incompatible with the
   current r-base, causing FTBFS for packages build‑depending on it (see the
   recent RC bugs opened by Santiago and Sebastian).  This currently blocks
   rebuild‑based progress.

I see the following technical options:

 * Extend Breaks from r-base against known‑incompatible r-cran- core packages
   (e.g. rlang, vctrs, others as identified), to limit invalid partial upgrades
   during migration.

 * Bump the virtual R API package (e.g. r-api-4.0 → r-api-4.6), enforcing a
   clean rebuild boundary at the cost of rebuilding a lot packages that do not
   require it.  This said, from my side, it is just a shell loop of source uploads
   running unattened.

 * Rebuild affected packages via binNMUs, selectively or broadly (currently
   constrained by r-cran-rcpp for some of them).

 * Ask the Release Team to force‑hint r-base into testing and let r-cran packages
   migrate later, accepting temporary breakage.

It looks to me that most options likely require declaring an R 4.6 transition
explicitly, both to reflect the current archive state and to align with Release
Team processes.

The mass architecture-restriction that I did not finish in time aggravates the
problem, but completing it will not solve alone the issue of r-base migration
because of the partial upgrade issue.

Dirk, I noted your activity upstream regarding the issue between Rcpp and the
latest R 4.6 release candidate, which prevents the rebuild or update of a bunch
of packages that would need it in most scenarios. What solution are you
envisioning?

Have a nice day,

Charles

messages.subject: R 4.6.0 and its 'binary' transition
messages.subject_clean: R 4.6.0 and its 'binary' transition
messages.body_plain:
R 4.6.0 came out on Friday, and following three weekly prerelease mapping the
upstream 'alpha', 'beta', and 'rc' stages, was updated on Friday as well.

With the release, (upstream team) R Core made some choices about symbols in
public headers that are the same time defensible (at least in theory), yet
(in practice) also questioned by some folks with experience around R (myself
included) and/or release management.

In short, 'public headers' were cleaned up by removing some previously
exported symbols (both functions and variables).  That obviously breaks some
things at compile-time. Yet at the same time it is _not_ an 'R API breakage'
as R 4.0.0 was.  Many packages built under any version past 4.0.0 still load
as can be checked easily. Packages without compiled code--by far the
majority--are also obviously unaffected by header changes. So what exactly is
the extend?

I had promised myself to do a little bit of data-driven digging, and have
done a first pass of that now over at a public repo that also has more
context than this short email:

   https://github.com/eddelbuettel/R-4.6.0-binary-transition

And we look good!! I used a GitHub code search to find packages checking for
'before or after 4.6.0', installed these and tested if they load. 'Known
suspects' such as `rlang` or `data.table` load fine in unstable which is
pretty nice!!  We did well so far.  I only found package `lobstr` to require
a rebuild which we can clearly do.

I need a bit of a break now after having spent some hours on this yesterday
and today, but I think I will go back to the container-based approach and
'simply' try to install and load each of our 183 (per a different thread in
the BTS) packages with compiled code. Maybe tomorrow. Spot-checking some
packages does not reveal any cause for concern.

So if you care about the topic, and have a minute maybe glance at the repo
and try the code. I can expand it and explain it more detail so feel free to
ask here or in an issue---but I just wanted to get a first email out.

Last but not least if 'we all' were to decide we really need a new tag and
full rebuild then I can of course adjust r-base-core. I just don't think we
need it, and I feel I now have to the empirical 'proof' for it.

Cheers, Dirk

-- 
Dirk Eddelbuettel | edd at debian.org | http://dirk.eddelbuettel.com

  Execution halted

'SET_GROWABLE_BIT' is one of those accessors now outlawd.
